newsitem.title: USA: Oil, grain prices fall, coffee stay strong.
newsitem.headline: Oil, grain prices fall, coffee stay strong.

text.p: Oil prices fell Friday despite a brutal cold snap as heating oil supplies were now seen as adequate to prevent any shortages.
In other markets, grain prices fell but coffee and lumber prices rose. The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 commodity futures ended 0.84 point lower at 241.63.

Meteorologists Friday forecast temperatures to fall 10 to 20 degrees below normal this weekend in the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market. In the Midwest, wind chill indexes dropped lower than 30 degrees below zero as artic air gripped much of the region.
In recent weeks, worries about heating oil supplies supported prices, but stocks now appears to have recovered.
"Despite the colder weather, the physical supply appears to be adequate," said William Brown of trading firm W.H. Brown in New York.

The American Petroleum Institute this week said that as of Jan. 10 stocks of distillates, which include heating oil and diesel, were only 350,000 barrels below levels of a year earlier. That compared to an almost 20 million-barrel gap last August.

On the New York Mercantile Exchange, February heating oil ended down 1.48 cents at 68.44 cents a gallon. February gasoline ended down 0.60 cent a gallon at 68.09 cents and February crude down 11 cents at $25.41 a barrel.

"One would anticipate heating oil to rise given that the coldest temperatures of the season are coming this weekend. But heating oil's failure to perform even just a little bit is weighing down the (energy) complex," said Andy Lebow, dealer with E.D. & F. Man International Inc.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, grain prices ended lower as traders judged prices too high to keep attracting export business. March wheat closed down 6-3/4 cents a bushel at $3.80-1/2 and March corn down 1/4 cent at $2.73-1/4.
"There's been wheat business, but not from the U.S., mainly Australian and French," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.

European grain traders Friday said Australia had sold 1.5 million metric tons of wheat to Iran, while Canada announced a deal to sell Thai flour millers at least a million tons of wheat over the next five years.

Corn prices were pressured in part by reports that Memphis, Tenn.-based analytical firm Sparks Cos. had forecast U.S. corn planted area this year at 81.5 million acres. U.S. farmers planted 79.5 million acres last year.
"The Sparks corn number was a little high and that put a little pressure on December corn," said analyst Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter.
January soybeans closed 1-1/2 cents lower at $7.46 a bushel as some forecasters predicted less rain for dry Brazilian fields.

At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee futures hit an eight-month high for the fourth consecutive session Friday as news that a Colombian dockworkers strike remained unsettled sparked speculative buying.
March coffee closed at 124.00 cents a pound, up 0.95 cent.

A Colombian coffee official said Friday the work stoppage had delayed the export of about 160,000 132-pound bags of coffee. Labor Ministry officials were due to arrive Friday in the Colombian port of Buenaventura in a bid to negotiate an end to the strike.
About 60 percent of Colombia's coffee exports are shipped through Buenaventura. Colombia is the No. 2 coffee exporter after Brazil.
At the New York Cotton Exchange, March frozen concentrated orange juice closed down 0.50 cent at 79.90 cents per pound as traders shrugged off a cold weather threat to Florida citrus.

"This will be the coldest night of the winter season down there, but probably not cold enough to do any damage," David Taylor of Weather Services Corp. said. "They are also well ahead in harvesting the fruit."
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, March lumber closed up the allowable $10 daily trading limit at $425.50 per thousand board feet.
"There is anticipation the weather is going to improve next week and maybe retail demand and pricing is going to improve," said Neil Schmaedick, Forest Products analyst for Smith Barney.
